items.followUp: What is one common source of biomass energy?

rubric.why: Identifies biomass as biological or organic material.
rubric.description: States that biomass consists of organic material from plants or animals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the biological/organic source.

accept: energy from plant and animal matter
rubric.why: Explains that energy is obtained from the biomass material.
rubric.description: Defines biomass energy as energy obtained from biomass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that energy is obtained from this material.

modelAnswer: Biomass is organic material obtained from plants and animals, including their waste.
Biomass energy is the energy obtained from this material.
followUp?A common source of biomass energy is wood, crop waste, or animal waste.

rubric.why: Identifies the SI unit of power.
rubric.description: Names the watt as the unit of power.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the unit.

rubric.why: Gives the defining rate of energy transfer or work.
rubric.description: Defines one watt as one joule of work done per second.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

modelAnswer: The SI unit of power is the watt (W).
One watt is the power when one joule of work is done in one second.

items.followUp: Write the formula for Young's modulus and name its SI unit.

rubric.why: States the defining ratio for Young's modulus.
rubric.description: Gives Young's modulus as the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio.

rubric.why: Includes the condition under which the ratio is defined.
rubric.description: States that the ratio applies within the elastic limit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the elastic-limit condition.

modelAnswer: Young's modulus is the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain within the elastic limit.
Young's modulus = longitudinal stress / longitudinal strain.

items.followUp: What instrument measures atmospheric pressure, and what is strain?

rubric.why: Identifies the instrument used to measure atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Defines a barometer as an instrument for measuring atmospheric pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the instrument and its function.

rubric.why: Gives the defining ratio for strain.
rubric.description: Defines strain as the change in dimension divided by the original dimension.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio.

modelAnswer: A barometer is an instrument used to measure atmospheric pressure.
Strain is the ratio of the change in a body's dimension to its original dimension.

items.followUp: State one difference between heat and temperature.

rubric.why: Describes heat as energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
rubric.description: States that heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of heat.

rubric.why: Describes temperature as a measure of hotness or coldness.
rubric.description: States that temperature measures the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of temperature.

modelAnswer: Heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body because of a temperature difference.
Temperature is the measure of the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.

items.followUp: Using a velocity-time graph, derive the first equation of motion, v = u + at.

rubric.why: Shows or describes the required velocity-time graph.
rubric.description: Draws a straight-line velocity-time graph from initial velocity Vi at time zero to final velocity v at time t.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the graph with correctly labelled axes and endpoints.

rubric.why: Uses the area under the graph to represent displacement.
rubric.description: Writes the trapezium-area expression for displacement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct area relation.

rubric.why: Uses the definition of acceleration to relate the velocities.
rubric.description: Rearranges the acceleration relation to express v in terms of Vi, a, and t.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct acceleration relation.

rubric.why: Completes the substitution and obtains the required equation.
rubric.description: Substitutes v = Vi + at into the displacement expression and gives the second equation of motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final equation.

modelAnswer: Draw a velocity-time graph with time t on the horizontal axis and velocity v on the vertical axis; mark the straight line from (0, Vi) to (t, v).
The displacement S is the area under the velocity-time graph.
S = area of trapezium = 1/2 (Vi + v)t.
Acceleration, a = (v − Vi)/t, so v = Vi + at.
Substitute v = Vi + at: S = 1/2 (Vi + Vi + at)t.
Therefore, S = Vit + 1/2 at².

items.followUp: A 4 kg body moving at 12 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest in 3 s. Find the force on it.

rubric.why: Records the given quantities and the final velocity for a stopped body.
rubric.description: Identifies the mass, initial velocity, final velocity, and stopping time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the given data.

rubric.why: Uses the equations connecting acceleration, velocity change, time, and force.
rubric.description: Selects the acceleration and force relations needed to solve the problem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the acceleration relation and 1 mark for the force relation.

rubric.why: Substitutes the values with units and obtains the signed force.
rubric.description: Shows the correct numerical substitution and force calculation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct substitution and calculation.

rubric.why: States the force magnitude and direction, or the signed force.
rubric.description: Gives a force of 25 N opposite to the direction of motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final force and direction.

modelAnswer: Given: mass m = 5 kg, initial velocity u = 10 m s⁻¹, final velocity v = 0 m s⁻¹, time t = 2 s.
Acceleration: a = (v − u)/t.
Force: F = ma.
The required force has magnitude 25 N and acts opposite to the body's motion.

items.followUp: Derive the relation for the gravitational potential energy gained by a body raised through height h.

accept: energy due to position or configuration
rubric.why: Defines potential energy in terms of position or configuration.
rubric.description: Defines potential energy as energy possessed by a body due to its position or configuration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Sets up the work done in raising the body.
rubric.description: States that the work done against gravity equals force multiplied by vertical displacement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the work relation.

rubric.why: Identifies the force against which work is done as the body's weight.
rubric.description: Uses the gravitational force F = mg.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the weight.

rubric.why: Combines the work relation with weight to obtain the potential-energy formula.
rubric.description: Derives and states gravitational potential energy as mgh.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final relation.

modelAnswer: Potential energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its position or configuration.
When a body of mass m is raised through height h, the work done against gravity is W = force × displacement.
The force against gravity is the body's weight, F = mg.
Therefore, potential energy gained = work done = Fh = mgh.
Thus, PE = mgh.
